answer.rationale: The primary supply contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renewal, so doing nothing is not an option; a lapsed contract at 94% line utilization with zero buffer would immediately create delivery risk. Finance mandates an 18% cost reduction, which rules out a simple status-quo renewal at current pricing. However, switching vendors (memory_c2 shows it can work) introduces onboarding and integration risk we cannot absorb at 94% utilization with no buffer—any slip in the transition could stall the line. Adding a second source (memory_c3) is prudent for resilience but does not by itself meet the 18% cut on the primary line item and would split volume, weakening leverage. Deferring (memory_c5) is not viable because the contract does not auto-renew; there is nothing to defer into. That leaves negotiate_terms as the single action that directly addresses both constraints simultaneously: it keeps the incumbent relationship intact (no migration risk, no delivery interruption—consistent with memory_c1) while using the 14-day renewal window and the credible threat of competitive bids to extract the price and payment-term concessions finance requires. Memory_c4 confirms this playbook has worked before (benchmarking moved the incumbent on price and terms), and memory_c6 shows that layering a multi-year commitment can unlock volume pricing, giving us a lever to trade term length for unit-cost reduction without narrowing service scope. I am requesting verification of c6 and c4 specifically because the negotiation strategy depends on (a) whether multi-year volume pricing was genuinely unlocked and (b) whether the prior renegotiation yielded durable margin recovery, not a one-time concession. If either record contradicts the consolidated summary, I would fall back to a short-term renewal at current rates to protect the line and revisit the cost target next cycle.
